ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.

payload.proof_nl:
Fix k with 0 <= k <= n-1 and set D_k(q) := (-q^d;q^d)_k = product_{j=1}^k (1+q^{dj}). Since n ≡ 1 mod 2d, n is odd.

If k=0, then D_0(q)=1, so gcd(D_0(q),M_n(q))=1 in Z[q]. Assume now k>=1.

We first show that D_k(q) and M_n(q) have no common complex root. Let alpha be a complex root of M_n(q)=[n]_q Phi_n(q)^2. Then alpha is a root of [n]_q or of Phi_n(q). For positive n we have [n]_q=1+q+...+q^{n-1}; hence if [n]_alpha=0 then alpha != 1 and 0=(alpha-1)[n]_alpha=alpha^n-1, so alpha^n=1. If Phi_n(alpha)=0, then alpha is a primitive n-th root of unity by definition of the cyclotomic polynomial, so again alpha^n=1. Thus every complex root of M_n(q) satisfies alpha^n=1.

If alpha were also a root of D_k(q), then because D_k(q)=product_{j=1}^k (1+q^{dj}), there would exist j in {1,...,k} such that 1+alpha^{dj}=0, i.e. alpha^{dj}=-1. But then
1=(alpha^n)^{dj}=alpha^{ndj}=(alpha^{dj})^n=(-1)^n=-1,
because n is odd. This is impossible. So D_k(q) and M_n(q) have no common complex root.

Now any nonconstant common divisor in Z[q] of D_k(q) and M_n(q) would also be a nonconstant complex polynomial dividing both, hence would have a complex root common to both polynomials. Since no such common root exists, there is no nonconstant common divisor in Z[q]. Therefore gcd(D_k(q),M_n(q))=1 in Z[q] for every k with 0 <= k <= n-1.

Next, define
N_k(q):=[3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2}.
Because 3dk+r>0, we have [3dk+r]_q=1+q+...+q^{3dk+r-1} in Z[q]. Each q-Pochhammer factor in N_k(q) is a finite product of terms 1-q^m, so it lies in Z[q]. The exponent k(d-dk-2r)/2 is an integer by hypothesis, so q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2} lies in Q[q,q^{-1}]. Hence N_k(q) lies in Q[q,q^{-1}].

The no-common-root argument above also shows that D_k(q) has no nonconstant common divisor with M_n(q) in Q[q]. By the definition of the localization Loc_{M_n}, every such polynomial in Q[q] is inverted there; hence D_k(q)^{-1} belongs to Loc_{M_n}. Since Loc_{M_n} contains the base ring Q[q,q^{-1}], it also contains N_k(q). Therefore
A_{d,r,n,k}(q)=N_k(q) D_k(q)^{-1}
belongs to Loc_{M_n} for every k.

Because a localization is a ring, it is closed under finite sums. Hence
S_{d,r,n}(q)=sum_{k=0}^{n-1} A_{d,r,n,k}(q)
belongs to Loc_{M_n}.

Finally, n is odd, so r(1-n)/2 is an integer. Since rn>0, [rn]_q=1+q+...+q^{rn-1} lies in Z[q], and q^{r(1-n)/2} lies in Q[q,q^{-1}]. Thus
R_{d,r,n}(q)=[rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2}
lies in Q[q,q^{-1}], hence in Loc_{M_n}.

This proves all assertions of the lemma.

payload.statement_nl: Let [m]_q=(1-q^m)/(1-q), let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial, define M_n(q):=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2, and let Loc_{M_n} be the localization of Q[q,q^{-1}] obtained by inverting every polynomial V(q) in Q[q] with gcd(V(q),M_n(q))=1. For any parameter u and integer k>=0, let (u;q)_k:=∏_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-u q^j), and let (u,v,w;q)_k:=(u;q)_k(v;q)_k(w;q)_k. Suppose d and r are positive integers with gcd(d,r)=1 and r <= d, and suppose n>1 satisfies n ≡ 1 mod 2d. For 0<=k<=n-1, define A_{d,r,n,k}(q):=[3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2}/(-q^d;q^d)_k, where k(d-dk-2r)/2 is an integer because k(1-k) is even. Define S_{d,r,n}(q):=∑_{k=0}^{n-1} A_{d,r,n,k}(q), and define R_{d,r,n}(q):=[rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2}, where r(1-n)/2 is an integer because n is odd. Then for every k with 0<=k<=n-1, the denominator (-q^d;q^d)_k=∏_{j=1}^{k}(1+q^{dj}) is coprime in Z[q] to M_n(q). Consequently A_{d,r,n,k}(q) belongs to Loc_{M_n} for every k, the finite sum S_{d,r,n}(q) belongs to Loc_{M_n}, and R_{d,r,n}(q) belongs to Loc_{M_n}.

detailed_findings.finding: The root-exclusion argument is correct: if alpha is a root of M_n(q), then alpha^n=1, while alpha^{dj}=-1 from a root of 1+q^{dj}; since n is odd this gives 1=(alpha^{dj})^n=-1, impossible.
detailed_findings.location: common-root contradiction for D_k and M_n

detailed_findings.finding: The passage from 'no common complex root' to coprimeness in Z[q] is mathematically sound here; for full formal clarity one may note explicitly that D_k has constant term 1, so no nonunit constant common divisor can occur.
The localization-membership conclusions for A_{d,r,n,k}(q), S_{d,r,n}(q), and R_{d,r,n}(q) follow correctly once D_k(q) is invertible and the remaining factors are shown to lie in Q[q,q^{-1}].

result_payload.reason: The proof matches the lemma’s intended role: it shows every complex root of M_n(q) is an n-th root of unity, excludes any common root with D_k(q)=(-q^d;q^d)_k using n odd, concludes the denominator is coprime to M_n, and then uses the localization definition to place each A_{d,r,n,k}(q), the finite sum S_{d,r,n}(q), and the target term R_{d,r,n}(q) in Loc_{M_n}. No material semantic drift or illegal dependency use is present.
